entry.title: attention is all you need, part 5: inference and the KV cache

link.title: attention is all you need, part 5: inference and the KV cache

entry.content:
Series · Attention is all you need 1Self-attention from scratch 2Multi-head attention and positions 3One encoder block 4The decoder, masking and training 5Inference and the KV cache

Part 4 finished the model: the decoder writes one word at a time, feeding each word back in. That loop is correct, but done naively it is slow. Every new word reruns the decoder over everything written so far.

This part is about inference: using a trained model, rather than training it. Almost everything that makes today’s chat models fast to run comes from one observation: with a causal mask, old positions never change. So their keys and values can be stored once and reused. That store is the KV cache.

Then we’ll look at the two main ways models shrink that cache, by sharing keys and values between heads (multi-query and grouped-query attention) and by limiting which past words a query may read (sliding windows and other attention patterns).

The scrolly figure below runs the decoder from part 4, with the cache, on the sentence you type. Every number is real.

The KV cache, step by step

Part 4’s generation loop, counted. At step \(k\), the decoder reads \(k\) tokens and computes queries, keys and values for all \(k\) of them, in every layer. Only the last position’s output is used to pick the next word.

Each row of the grid is one step; each cell is one position the decoder has to compute. Writing \(n\) words costs

\[1 + 2 + \cdots + n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}\]

positions: the work grows with the square of the length.

The mask makes old positions frozen. Position \(i\) only reads positions \(0 \dots i\). When a new word arrives at the end, nothing before it changes: the keys and values of the earlier positions come out exactly as they did last step.

So keep them. At each step, compute the keys and values of the new token only, append them to a cache, and let its query read the whole cache. The grid shrinks to its diagonal: \(n\) positions instead of \(n(n+1)/2\).

Cross-attention’s keys and values never change. They come from the encoder’s output, and the encoder reads the source sentence once. So before writing a single word, the decoder computes \(K = \text{memory} \cdot W_K\) and \(V = \text{memory} \cdot W_V\) for each layer and head, and keeps them for the whole generation.

Running the whole prompt through the model in one pass before writing is called prefill. In a decoder-only model like GPT, the prompt goes through the decoder itself, and prefill fills its self-attention cache with one row per prompt token.

A decode step. The decoder is fed a single token: the word it picked last step, plus the positional encoding for its place in the sentence. (Not position 0. A real implementation has to keep count.)

That one row of 8 numbers goes through \(W_Q\), \(W_K\) and \(W_V\) as in part 1, giving one query, one key and one value: each a single row of 4 numbers.

Append, don’t recompute. The new key goes to the bottom of the key cache, the new value to the bottom of the value cache. The rows above are what earlier steps put there, untouched.

This happens in every self-attention head of every decoder layer. The figure shows layer 1, head 1. Scroll on to watch it fill.

Attention with a single query. The new query is scored against every cached key, its own included:

\[\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{q K_{\text{cache}}^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V_{\text{cache}}\]

That’s equation (1) from part 1 with a \(1 \times 4\) query instead of an \(n \times 4\) one. No mask is needed: the cache only holds the past.

The rest of the block (Add & Norm, cross-attention, the feed-forward network) also runs on just this one row.

The cache is not an approximation. The table runs both versions on your sentence: part 4’s full pass at every step, and the cached decode step. They pick the same words with the same probabilities, down to the last digit.

The trade: we’ve swapped repeated computation for memory. That memory is what the rest of this post is about.

The full cache. Every self-attention head in every decoder layer keeps a K and a V. In our toy that’s 2 layers × 2 heads × (4 + 4) numbers = 32 numbers per token.

In a real model it’s far more. Llama 2 7B keeps 2 × 32 layers × 32 heads × 128 = 262,144 numbers per token: half a megabyte at 16 bits. A 4,096-token conversation needs 2 GiB of cache on top of the weights.

Sharing keys and values between heads

The paper gives every attention head its own \(W_K\) and \(W_V\), so every head caches its own keys and values. That’s multi-head attention (MHA). But heads are mostly free to differ in their queries: what each one looks for. Do they each need their own keys and values?

  • Multi-query attention (MQA, Shazeer, 2019): all query heads share a single key head and a single value head. The cache shrinks by the number of heads, often 32× or more. Quality can drop somewhat.
  • Grouped-query attention (GQA, Ainslie et al., 2023): the middle ground. Query heads are split into groups, and each group shares one key and value head. With 8 groups, the authors found quality close to multi-head attention with speed close to multi-query.

Each query head still computes its own scores and weights; only the \(K\) and \(V\) they read are shared. Most open models since 2023 use GQA: Llama 2 70B, Llama 3, Mistral 7B and others pair 32 or 64 query heads with 8 key/value heads.

How much memory is that? For one sequence, the cache holds

\[2 \cdot L \cdot h_{kv} \cdot d_{head} \cdot n \cdot b \text{ bytes}\]

where the 2 is for K and V, \(L\) is the number of layers, \(h_{kv}\) the number of key/value heads, \(d_{head}\) the numbers per head, \(n\) the tokens so far and \(b\) the bytes per number (2, for 16-bit numbers).

Pick a model, a context length and a number of sequences served at once:

Try Llama 2 7B at its full 4,096 tokens and 32 sequences: 64 GiB of cache, for a model whose weights take about 13.5 GB. At long contexts the cache, not the model, decides how much a GPU can serve.

Which keys a query may read

So far we’ve met two attention patterns. The encoder’s self-attention is full: every word reads every word. The decoder’s is causal: every word reads only itself and the past. Cross-attention is a third kind: queries from one sequence, keys and values from another.

Patterns are just masks: which (query, key) pairs get a score, and which get \(-\infty\) (part 4). Changing the mask changes both the cost and what the cache has to keep. Rows are queries, columns are keys, and dark cells are pairs that get computed:

  • Sliding window (Longformer, Mistral 7B): each token reads only the last \(w\) tokens. Cost per token is fixed, and the cache can be a ring buffer of \(w\) rows. Information from further back still flows, but indirectly: layer 2 reads tokens that read the \(w\) before them, so after \(L\) layers a token can be influenced by about \(L \times w\) positions.
  • Attention sinks (StreamingLLM): trained models put a lot of attention on the first few tokens, whatever they are, as a place to park weight they don’t need. Evict those from a sliding window and the model falls apart. Keep the first 4 plus the window, and the authors ran Llama 2 stably on 4 million tokens.
  • Prefix (studied in the T5 paper): the prompt attends in both directions, like an encoder, and only the answer is causal. It’s a halfway house between the paper’s encoder–decoder and a decoder-only model.
  • Sparse patterns (Child et al., 2019): each token reads a local window plus every \(k\)-th earlier token, so two hops can reach anywhere at a cost of about \(n\sqrt{n}\) instead of \(n^2\).

Some models mix them. Gemma 2 alternates sliding-window and full-attention layers, and Gemma 3 uses five sliding-window layers (of 1,024 tokens) for each full one, so most layers have a small cache and a few still see everything.

Going deeper

Prefill and decode are different kinds of work

A GPU can do arithmetic far faster than it can read memory. An H100 does about 990 trillion 16-bit operations per second but reads about 3.35 trillion bytes per second: roughly 300 operations in the time it takes to read one byte.

  • Prefill pushes the whole prompt through at once. Every weight that is read gets used for hundreds or thousands of tokens, so the chip stays busy with arithmetic. This is compute-bound, like training.
  • Decode pushes one token per sequence. Every weight read from memory is used for one multiply-add per sequence, a couple of operations per two-byte number. The chip spends most of its time waiting for memory. This is memory-bound.

Serving many sequences at once (batching) helps decode, because they all share the weights: one read of \(W_Q\) serves the whole batch. The cache can’t be shared, though: every sequence reads its own. At long contexts reading the cache dominates, which is why shrinking it with GQA or MQA speeds up decoding, not just saves memory. Much of Pope et al. (2022) is this analysis, at scale.

Multi-head latent attention: cache something smaller

DeepSeek-V2 (2024) keeps 128 query heads and effectively 128 key/value heads, but caches neither keys nor values. Each token’s vector is first squeezed into a small latent vector,

\[c = x\, W_{down}, \qquad c \in \mathbb{R}^{512},\]

and that’s what gets cached. Each head’s keys and values are \(c\, W_{up}^{K}\) and \(c\, W_{up}^{V}\). Because matrix products can be regrouped, \(W_{up}^{K}\) can be folded into \(W_Q\) ahead of time (and \(W_{up}^{V}\) into \(W_O\)), so the full keys are never written out.

There’s one catch: RoPE (next section) rotates keys by position, and a rotation stuck between \(W_{up}^{K}\) and \(W_Q\) breaks the folding. So DeepSeek-V2 also caches one small 64-number key that carries the position. That’s 576 numbers per token per layer, against 32,768 for 128 full heads: 57 times smaller. The paper reports a 93% smaller cache than its previous 67B model.

Positions inside the cache

Our toy adds the sinusoidal position encoding to the input, as the paper does, so a cached key already “knows” its position. Most models today use rotary embeddings (RoPE) instead: rather than adding a position to the input, they rotate each query and key by an angle proportional to its position, inside every attention layer.

That works well with a cache. A key’s rotation depends only on its own position, so it’s rotated once and stored rotated. And part 2’s rotation trick does the rest: the score between a query at position \(p\) and a key at \(k\) depends only on the distance \(p - k\), however long the cache gets.

FlashAttention and the online softmax

The cache saves recomputation, but each step still reads every cached key and value. FlashAttention speeds up the attention computation itself by never writing the full score matrix to the GPU’s main memory: it reads \(K\) and \(V\) in blocks small enough for fast on-chip memory, and finishes each block before loading the next.

The hard part is the softmax, which seems to need every score before it can divide. The trick (Milakov & Gimelshein, 2018) is to keep a running maximum \(m\), a running sum \(\ell\) and a running output \(o\). For each new block of scores \(s_j\):

\[m' = \max(m,\, \max_j s_j)\] \[\ell' = e^{m - m'}\ell + \textstyle\sum_j e^{s_j - m'}\] \[o' = e^{m - m'}\, o + \textstyle\sum_j e^{s_j - m'}\, v_j\]

and the answer is \(o / \ell\) at the end. The factor \(e^{m - m'}\) rescales everything so far whenever a bigger score turns up. On the cached step in the figure above, done two keys at a time, it matches the direct softmax to about \(10^{-16}\), the last digit a computer keeps. FlashAttention is exact, not an approximation; it changes how much memory traffic attention needs, not what it computes.

PagedAttention: the cache as virtual memory

A server doesn’t know in advance how long each answer will be. Reserving a cache for the maximum length wastes most of it; vLLM found earlier systems used as little as a fifth of the memory they reserved. PagedAttention borrows the operating system’s answer: split the cache into small fixed-size blocks, hand them out as a sequence grows, and keep a table of where each sequence’s blocks are. Sequences that share a prompt can share its blocks. The authors report 2–4× more throughput at the same latency.

Speculative decoding: use part 4’s trick in reverse

Part 4 showed that one masked pass over a sentence gives the same predictions as writing it word by word. Speculative decoding uses that to break the one-word-per-pass limit. A small, fast model drafts a few words ahead. The big model then checks all of them in one pass, the way it would during training, and keeps the drafted words up to the first one it disagrees with, plus its own word at that point.

Every pass of the big model yields at least one word, and often several. With the right acceptance rule for sampling, the output follows exactly the big model’s distribution. The authors report 2–3× faster decoding on T5-XXL with identical outputs.

Choosing the next word

Part 4 always took the most likely word (greedy). Chat models usually sample from the probabilities instead, after reshaping them:

  • Temperature \(T\) divides the logits before the softmax: \(\text{softmax}(z / T)\). Below 1 sharpens the distribution towards greedy; above 1 flattens it. It’s the √d_k story from part 1 again: dividing scores changes how peaked a softmax is.
  • Top-k keeps only the \(k\) most likely words and renormalises.
  • Top-p or nucleus sampling (Holtzman et al., 2019) keeps the smallest set of words whose probabilities add up to \(p\). It’s a fixed share of the probability rather than a fixed number of words, so it adapts: few candidates when the model is sure, many when it isn’t.

None of these change the cache: they act only on the final probabilities.

Further reading

  • Noam Shazeer, Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need (2019): multi-query attention, and a clear cost analysis of incremental decoding.
  • Ainslie et al., GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints (2023).
  • Pope et al., Efficiently Scaling Transformer Inference (2022): prefill vs. decode, memory vs. compute, at scale.
  • Dao et al., FlashAttention (2022), and Kwon et al., PagedAttention (2023).
  • DeepSeek-AI, DeepSeek-V2 (2024), section 2.1: multi-head latent attention.

entry.title: attention is all you need, part 4: the decoder, masking and training

link.title: attention is all you need, part 4: the decoder, masking and training

entry.content:
Series · Attention is all you need 1Self-attention from scratch 2Multi-head attention and positions 3One encoder block 4The decoder, masking and training 5Inference and the KV cache

The first three parts built the encoder: it reads a sentence and turns each word into a vector shaped by the whole sentence. Part 3 ended with a stack of encoder blocks.

The paper’s Transformer was built for translation, so it also needs a way to write. That is the decoder, the right half of Figure 1. It reuses almost everything we’ve seen, with two changes:

  1. Its self-attention is masked, so a word can’t peek at the words that come after it.
  2. It adds cross-attention, where it reads the encoder’s output.

This part covers the decoder, the output layer, the loop that writes a sentence word by word, and how the whole thing is trained.

Our toy can’t translate: it has 35 words and has never been trained. So its task is the simplest one there is: copy the sentence. The encoder reads “the cat sat on the mat” and the decoder should write it back. The arithmetic is the same as for translation; only the training data would differ.

The decoder, step by step

Here are both halves. On the left, the encoder from part 3. On the right, the decoder.

A decoder block has three sublayers instead of two, each wrapped in Add & Norm:

  1. masked self-attention over the words written so far,
  2. cross-attention, which reads the encoder’s output (the blue line),
  3. the same kind of feed-forward network as the encoder.

Like the encoder, the paper stacks N = 6 of them.

How is the decoder trained? We already know the right output, so we feed it in, moved one place to the right, with a start token <s> in front.

Then every position has a simple job: predict the word under it. After <s> comes the; after the comes cat; and so on.

This is called teacher forcing. All positions are trained at the same time, in one pass, which is much faster than generating word by word.

There’s a catch. If position 2 can attend to position 3, it can simply read the answer. The model would learn to copy instead of to predict.

So before the softmax, we add a mask: \(-\infty\) to every score above the diagonal, 0 everywhere else.

\[\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} + M\right) V\]

Since \(e^{-\infty} = 0\), those words get exactly zero weight. Each row is a word that can only see itself and the words before it, just like when the model writes for real. (Why not just zero them afterwards?)

The second sublayer looks across. It is ordinary multi-head attention with one difference: the queries come from the decoder, but the keys and values come from the encoder’s output.

\[\text{Attention}(Q_{\text{decoder}},\, K_{\text{encoder}},\, V_{\text{encoder}})\]

So each word the decoder is writing asks: which source words matter for me right now? In translation, this is where the model lines up chat with cat. Hover or tap a word on the left.

Our weights are random, so the lines here don’t mean anything yet. There’s no mask: the whole source sentence is known from the start.

From vectors back to words. The decoder’s last row is a vector of 8 numbers. To turn it into a word, we score it against every word in the vocabulary.

The paper does this with the embedding table itself: the logits are \(y\,E^\top\), a dot product with each word’s embedding. Reusing \(E\) saves weights and ties input and output words together.

A softmax turns the logits into probabilities. (My post on next-word prediction is all about this last step.)

After training, the decoder writes one word at a time. Start with <s>. Run the decoder, pick the likeliest word, append it, run again. Stop at the end token </s>.

The encoder runs once; the decoder runs once per word.

Here is our toy doing exactly that. Its output is nonsense, because it hasn’t learned anything. A trained model runs the very same loop and gets the copy right. Real systems usually pick with beam search (the paper uses a beam of 4) rather than always taking the top word.

Training measures how wrong the model is. At each position, compare the model’s probabilities with the right answer using cross-entropy:

\[\text{loss} = -\sum_{w} \text{target}(w) \cdot \log p(w)\]

The paper uses label smoothing with \(\epsilon = 0.1\). Instead of asking for 100% on the right word, the target is 90%, with the other 10% spread over every other word. The paper notes that this makes the model less sure of itself, which hurts one measure (perplexity) but improves the translations (BLEU).

Our untrained model gives mat almost nothing, so the loss is high. Training uses its gradient to nudge every weight, over and over, to bring it down.

How big should each nudge be? The paper uses the Adam optimiser with a learning rate that changes as training goes on:

\[\text{lr} = \frac{\min\!\left(s^{-0.5},\ s \cdot w^{-1.5}\right)}{\sqrt{d_{model}}}\]

where \(s\) is the training step and \(w = 4000\) is the number of warmup steps.

For the first 4000 steps it grows in a straight line. Big steps at the very start, when the weights are random, tend to blow training up. After that it shrinks like \(1/\sqrt{\text{step}}\), so the model settles down.

The base model trained for 100,000 steps, about 12 hours on 8 GPUs.

And that’s the whole model. Every box in the paper’s Figure 1 is something we’ve now computed by hand:

  • embeddings and positional encodings (parts 1 and 2),
  • scaled dot-product and multi-head attention (parts 1 and 2),
  • Add & Norm and the feed-forward network (part 3),
  • masking, cross-attention, the output layer and training (this part).

Putting it all together

Here’s the full model, in the order the data moves:

  1. Encoder. Embed the source words, add positions, and run \(N\) encoder blocks.
  2. Decoder. Embed the words written so far, add positions, and run \(N\) decoder blocks. Each one does masked self-attention, cross-attention to the encoder’s output, and a feed-forward network.
  3. Output. Multiply the last decoder vector by \(E^\top\) and take the softmax to get the next word.
  4. Training. Teacher forcing, cross-entropy with label smoothing, and Adam with warmup.

The paper’s base model has \(d_{model} = 512\), 8 heads, \(d_{ff} = 2048\) and \(N = 6\): about 65 million weights. Our toy has a few thousand. The arithmetic is the same.

What came next

The paper’s encoder–decoder design split into two families almost at once:

  • Encoder only, like BERT (2018): just the left stack, for understanding text.
  • Decoder only, like GPT (2018): just the right stack, without cross-attention. Masked self-attention and the generation loop from this post are, more or less, how today’s chat models write.

The core of every one of them is the equation from part 1.

Going deeper

Why −∞ before the softmax, and not 0 after?

Adding \(-\infty\) to a score makes its \(e^{x}\) exactly 0, so the softmax of a masked row is

\[p_j = \frac{e^{x_j}}{\sum_{l \le i} e^{x_l}} \quad (j \le i)\]

and \(p_j = 0\) for \(j > i\).

That is exactly a softmax over the allowed words only. The row still adds up to 1, and future words play no part in it.

Now try it the other way: take the normal softmax, then set the future weights to 0. The row no longer adds up to 1. Worse, the future scores were in the denominator, so the weights that are left still carry a trace of the future words. The model could learn to read that trace.

In real code the mask is usually a large negative number such as \(-10^9\) rather than true \(-\infty\). If a whole row is masked (it happens with padding), true infinities give \(0/0\), which is NaN. The causal mask always leaves the diagonal open, so our toy can use real \(-\infty\).

Why one masked pass equals writing word by word

With the mask, the output at position \(i\) depends only on positions \(0 \dots i\). Every other part of the decoder works on each position on its own, or looks only backwards. So running the decoder on the whole sentence at once gives each position exactly the same vector as running it on just the words up to that point. In our toy the two agree to the last digit.

That’s what makes teacher forcing work: one pass trains all \(n\) predictions at once. It also explains a trick every chat model uses when generating. Earlier positions never change, so their keys and values can be stored and reused (the KV cache). Each new word then costs one new row, rather than a rerun of the whole sentence. Part 5 draws it step by step.

What label smoothing does to the loss

With a smoothed target \(t\), the loss \(-\sum_w t(w) \log p(w)\) is smallest when the model’s probabilities equal the target exactly, \(p = t\). Even then it isn’t 0: its lowest value is the target’s own entropy. For the paper’s shared vocabulary of about 37,000 tokens that floor is about 1.38; for our 35 words it is 0.68.

So the best the model can do is put 90% on the right word, never 100%. Without smoothing, the loss keeps falling as the right word’s logit grows, so the model is rewarded for becoming ever more certain. Smoothing removes that reward. The paper reports that this makes the model less certain (worse perplexity) but improves both accuracy and BLEU.

Why warm up?

The paper doesn’t say. There are two common explanations, and they don’t exclude each other:

  • Adam needs data first. Adam divides each step by a running estimate of how big the gradients are. In the first few steps that estimate rests on very few samples, so some steps come out far too large. A small learning rate keeps those early steps safe (Liu et al., 2019).
  • Post-norm is touchy. With LayerNorm after each add, as in the paper, gradients near the output are large at the start of training. Moving the LayerNorm inside the residual branch (pre-norm) tames them, and such models can train without any warmup (Xiong et al., 2020).

For the record, the paper’s Adam settings were \(\beta_1 = 0.9\), \(\beta_2 = 0.98\), \(\epsilon = 10^{-9}\). The schedule peaks at step 4000, at \(512^{-0.5} \cdot 4000^{-0.5} \approx 7.0 \times 10^{-4}\).

One table for three jobs

The paper uses a single matrix for three jobs: the encoder’s input embedding, the decoder’s input embedding, and the final layer that turns vectors into word scores (Press & Wolf, 2016). With 37,000 tokens and \(d = 512\), each copy would be about 19 million weights, so sharing saves tens of millions.

It also makes sense: a word’s score is high when the decoder’s vector points the same way as that word’s embedding. The paper also multiplies the embeddings by \(\sqrt{d_{model}}\) on the way in. A common explanation: a table shared with the output layer starts with small numbers, and the scaling keeps the words from being drowned out by the positional encodings.

Greedy decoding vs. beam search

Our loop takes the single most likely word every time (greedy decoding). That can paint the model into a corner: a word that looks best now can lead to a worse sentence overall.

Beam search keeps the best few partial sentences at every step instead of one. The paper keeps 4. A sentence’s score is the sum of its words’ log-probabilities, which favours short outputs, since every extra word adds a negative number. A length penalty (\(\alpha = 0.6\) in the paper) corrects for that.

Further reading

  • Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need, sections 3.1–3.4 (decoder and output) and 5 (training).
  • Harvard NLP, The Annotated Transformer: the full model and training loop in PyTorch, including the mask and label smoothing.
  • Andrej Karpathy, Let’s build GPT: from scratch, in code, spelled out: a decoder-only Transformer, built live.
  • Jay Alammar, The Illustrated GPT-2: the decoder-only family, in pictures.

entry.title: attention is all you need, part 3: one encoder block

link.title: attention is all you need, part 3: one encoder block

entry.content:
Series · Attention is all you need 1Self-attention from scratch 2Multi-head attention and positions 3One encoder block 4The decoder, masking and training 5Inference and the KV cache

Part 2 finished the multi-head attention sublayer. On its own it lets words share information, but a Transformer needs a few more parts around it to train well and to do something with that information.

Those parts make up one encoder block, the left half of the paper’s Figure 1. There are three new ideas, all small:

  1. Residual connections: add a sublayer’s input back to its output.
  2. Layer normalisation: rescale each word’s numbers to mean 0 and variance 1.
  3. A feed-forward network: two matrix multiplies with a ReLU between them, applied to each word on its own.

Same toy model as before, now with positions added. Edit the sentence and every matrix below recomputes.

Inside the block, step by step

Here is the whole block. Read it from the bottom up, the way the data flows.

The input is \(X + PE\) from part 2. It goes through multi-head attention, then Add & Norm, then a feed-forward network, then Add & Norm again.

The lines running up the right side skip around each sublayer. They are the residual connections. The dashed frame with “× N” means the paper stacks N = 6 of these blocks.

The first “Add”. Take the block’s input X and the output of attention, and add them, number by number:

\[X + \text{MultiHead}(X)\]

This is a residual connection (from ResNet, 2015). Attention doesn’t have to rebuild each word’s vector from scratch. It only has to learn a change to add on top.

That makes deep stacks much easier to train (here’s why). If a block has nothing useful to add, it can learn to add almost nothing, and the word passes through unharmed.

Then “Norm”. For each word separately, compute the mean and variance of its 8 numbers. Subtract the mean and divide by the square root of the variance:

\[\text{LayerNorm}(x) = \gamma \cdot \frac{x - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}} + \beta\]

The number line underneath shows one row before and after. The dots keep their order and their relative spacing; they are just shifted and squeezed so the mean sits at 0 and the spread is 1. Hover or tap a word to see its row.

Without this, numbers can drift bigger and bigger as they pass through the layers. \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) are learned per column, so the model can undo the squeeze where it helps. Ours start at 1 and 0.

The second sublayer is a tiny neural network. First, multiply each word’s 8 numbers by \(W_1\), an 8 × 16 matrix. Every word grows to 16 numbers.

Then apply ReLU, which keeps positive numbers and turns negative ones into 0. Watch the hidden matrix: at the end of the step every blue (negative) cell turns grey: it is now 0.

This is the only non-linear step in the block apart from softmax. Without it, two matrix multiplies in a row would collapse into one.

Then multiply by \(W_2\), a 16 × 8 matrix, to get back to 8 numbers per word. Together that is the paper’s equation (2):

\[\text{FFN}(x) = \max(0,\, x W_1 + b_1)\, W_2 + b_2\]

Notice what this step doesn’t do: it never mixes rows. Every word goes through the same two matrices on its own. The paper calls it position-wise. Attention moves information between words; the feed-forward network works on what each word has gathered.

In the paper the hidden layer has 2048 numbers per word, against 512 for the model. That makes the feed-forward network about two thirds of each block’s weights.

The same trick a second time. Add the feed-forward network’s input to its output, then apply LayerNorm:

\[\text{LayerNorm}(x + \text{FFN}(x))\]

The result is the block’s output. It has exactly the same shape as the input: one row of 8 numbers per word.

Same shape in, same shape out. That means the output of one block can be fed straight into the next.

Each block has its own weights, so each one can refine the vectors a bit more. Our toy uses 2 blocks; the paper uses N = 6, and large modern models use 100 or more.

The output of the last block is the encoder’s final answer: one vector per word, each one shaped by the whole sentence. In part 4 the decoder reads it.

The whole block in two lines

Writing \(x\) for the input of a block, the paper’s encoder layer is:

\[h = \text{LayerNorm}(x + \text{MultiHead}(x))\] \[\text{out} = \text{LayerNorm}(h + \text{FFN}(h))\]

All sublayers, and the embeddings too, produce \(d_{model} = 512\) numbers per word in the paper (8 in our toy), precisely so these additions line up.

Two details from the paper I left out of the figure. Dropout is applied to each sublayer’s output before the add, with rate 0.1 in training. And the order shown here, add first and then normalise (“post-norm”), is the original. Most models today normalise first, \(x + \text{Sublayer}(\text{LayerNorm}(x))\) (“pre-norm”), because it trains more stably in deep stacks.

Going deeper

Why residual connections help learning

Training works backwards. The loss sends a gradient back through every layer, and each layer multiplies it by its own derivative. With a residual connection, a sublayer computes \(y = x + F(x)\), so its derivative is

\[\frac{\partial y}{\partial x} = I + \frac{\partial F}{\partial x}\]

The \(I\) (the identity) is the important part. Going back through \(N\) blocks multiplies \(N\) of these together. Multiply out the brackets and one of the terms is just \(I \cdot I \cdots I\): a path where the gradient reaches the first block untouched, however deep the stack.

Without the skip, the gradient is a product of \(N\) derivatives \(\partial F / \partial x\). Products of many factors tend to shrink towards zero or blow up, which is why very deep networks were so hard to train before ResNet. Veit et al. (2016) give another way to see it: a residual network behaves like many shallow networks of different depths, added together.

Why LayerNorm and not BatchNorm?

BatchNorm, common in image models, normalises each feature across all the examples in a batch. LayerNorm normalises each word across its own features. For text, LayerNorm is the better fit:

  • Sentences in a batch have different lengths and are padded. Batch statistics would mix in padding and depend on which other sentences happen to share the batch.
  • When generating, there is often only one sentence, so there is no batch to average over.
  • LayerNorm treats every word on its own, so it computes exactly the same thing in training and in use.

Where the weights live

Count the weights in one block of the paper’s base model (\(d = 512\), \(d_{ff} = 2048\), ignoring the small biases and LayerNorm parameters):

  • attention: \(W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O\) are 4 matrices of \(d \times d\), so \(4d^2 \approx 1.05\) million.
  • feed-forward: \(W_1\) is \(d \times 4d\) and \(W_2\) is \(4d \times d\), so \(8d^2 \approx 2.1\) million.

The feed-forward network holds two thirds of each block’s weights, and does most of its arithmetic too.

What does the feed-forward network do?

Read equation (2) one hidden unit at a time. Each of the 2048 hidden units has a column of \(W_1\), which works like a key: its dot product with the word’s vector says how well the word matches some pattern. ReLU keeps only positive matches. The matching row of \(W_2\) is a value, added to the output in proportion to the match.

So the network is a big, fixed lookup: “if the word looks like this, add that”. Geva et al. (2021) found exactly this in trained models. In lower layers, keys tend to fire on surface patterns, such as text ending in a particular word; in higher layers, on topics. In the higher layers, the values push towards likely next words. It looks like attention, except the keys and values are learned once, rather than coming from the sentence.

Further reading

  • Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need, sections 3.1 (encoder stack) and 3.3 (feed-forward networks).
  • Ba, Kiros and Hinton, Layer Normalization (2016).
  • He et al., Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition (2015): where residual connections come from.
  • Xiong et al., On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture (2020): post-norm vs. pre-norm.

entry.title: attention is all you need, part 2: multi-head attention and positions

link.title: attention is all you need, part 2: multi-head attention and positions

entry.content:
Series · Attention is all you need 1Self-attention from scratch 2Multi-head attention and positions 3One encoder block 4The decoder, masking and training 5Inference and the KV cache

Part 1 built one attention head from scratch. It ended with two problems:

  1. Attention can’t tell word order. “The cat sat on the mat” and “mat the on sat cat the” look the same to it.
  2. One head can only ask one kind of question at a time.

The paper solves the first with positional encodings and the second with multi-head attention. Both are small ideas. Let’s see them with real numbers.

As before, this is the tiny model from part 1: 8 numbers per word and real arithmetic. The sentence is editable, and scrolling inside a step plays it.

Positions and heads, step by step

First, the problem. On the left is the output of an attention layer for our sentence. On the right is the same sentence reversed.

Every line joins a word to the same word in the other sentence. Their rows are exactly equal. The layer has no idea the order changed. It only moved the rows around.

That makes sense. Attention compares every word with every other word, and nothing in those comparisons says where a word is.

The fix: give each position its own fingerprint. The paper uses waves. Column \(2i\) of the encoding is a sine wave and column \(2i+1\) is a cosine, each at its own speed:

\[PE_{(pos,\,2i)} = \sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right)\] \[PE_{(pos,\,2i+1)} = \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right)\]

The first pair of waves wiggles fast and the last pair barely moves. Read down at any position (the blue line) and you get 8 heights. That is the position’s row of PE. No two positions have the same row.

Then we simply add. Each word’s row of X gets its position’s row of PE added to it, number by number.

Adding, not appending, keeps the size at 8 numbers. The word is still in there, and now the position is too. Two copies of the at positions 0 and 4 now get different rows.

From here on, every layer sees \(X + PE\) instead of X.

Run the same test again, this time with positions added.

Now the lines turn red and dashed: the same word gets a different output depending on where it stands. Word order finally matters.

(There is nothing special about reversing. Any other order would show the same thing.)

Why waves, and not just the numbers 0, 1, 2, …? Plain counting grows without limit, and the network would only ever see small numbers while training.

Waves stay between −1 and 1. They also have a nice property. Treat each sine/cosine pair as a point on a circle. Moving one position later turns the point by the same angle, wherever it starts.

So “the word just before me” is the same rotation at position 3 as at position 300. A weight matrix can learn to recognise it once and use it everywhere. (The proof is below.) The paper says the authors chose waves because they hoped the model could “easily learn to attend by relative positions”.

Now the second problem. sat wants to know who sat, but also where. One softmax row can’t put most of its weight on two places at once.

So the Transformer runs several heads side by side. Each head has its own \(W_Q\), \(W_K\) and \(W_V\) and runs its own attention, exactly as in part 1.

Our toy has 2 heads. Head 1 is the hand-wired one from part 1. Head 2 is random. Hover or tap a row to compare them. In a trained model every head learns a pattern of its own. Some track the previous word, some link a pronoun to its noun, and some just look at punctuation.

Each head is made smaller, so the total cost stays the same. With \(d_{model} = 8\) and 2 heads, each head works with \(d_k = 8 / 2 = 4\) numbers.

The heads’ outputs are placed side by side (“concatenated”) to get back to 8 numbers per word. Then one more matrix, \(W_O\), mixes them. The square brackets mean “side by side”:

\[\text{MultiHead}(X) = [\,\text{head}_1 \cdots \text{head}_h\,]\, W_O\]

The paper uses 8 heads of 64 numbers each: \(8 \times 64 = 512 = d_{model}\).

Was it worth it? The paper compares attention with recurrent layers. Drag the slider to change the number of words.

Attention compares every pair of words, so its work grows like \(n^2\). A recurrent layer does less work per word for long inputs, but it has to go one word after another: \(n\) steps, each waiting for the last.

For sentences shorter than \(d\) (512 in the paper), attention is both cheaper and fully parallel. That speed is a big part of why Transformers took over. The \(n^2\) cost for very long texts is why so much later research tries to make attention cheaper.

What we have so far

We now have the full multi-head attention sublayer of the paper:

  1. Add positions: \(X \leftarrow X + PE\).
  2. For each head h: \(\text{head}_h = \text{Attention}(X W_Q^h,\; X W_K^h,\; X W_V^h)\).
  3. Join the heads and mix: \(\text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \ldots, \text{head}_h)\, W_O\).

Its output has the same shape as its input: one row of \(d_{model}\) numbers per word.

One detail I glossed over: the paper also multiplies the embeddings by \(\sqrt{d_{model}}\) before adding positions, so the two have similar sizes. In this toy the embeddings already have about the right size, so I left that out.

Attention lets words share information, but it doesn’t do much with that information on its own. In part 3 we wrap it in the rest of an encoder block: residual connections, layer normalisation and a small feed-forward network.

Going deeper

Why a shift is a rotation

Take one sine/cosine pair with speed \(\omega\). Write \(a = \omega p\) for the angle at position \(p\), and \(b = \omega k\) for the extra angle after \(k\) more steps. The angle-addition rules say:

\[\sin(a + b) = \sin a \cos b + \cos a \sin b\] \[\cos(a + b) = \cos a \cos b - \sin a \sin b\]

In matrix form:

\[\begin{pmatrix} \sin(a+b) \\ \cos(a+b) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \cos b & \sin b \\ -\sin b & \cos b \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \sin a \\ \cos a \end{pmatrix}\]

The matrix in the middle is a rotation by the angle \(b = \omega k\). It depends on \(k\) but not on \(p\). So “\(k\) places later” is the same fixed matrix at every position. A weight matrix like \(W_Q\) multiplies by fixed matrices, so in principle it can learn “the word just before me” once and have it work everywhere.

Dot products only see distance

Here’s another consequence. Take the dot product of two position rows, \(PE(p)\) and \(PE(p+k)\). Each sine/cosine pair contributes \(\sin a \sin b + \cos a \cos b = \cos(a - b)\), so

\[PE(p) \cdot PE(p+k) = \sum_i \cos(\omega_i k)\]

This depends only on the distance \(k\), not on where you are. In our toy (\(d = 8\)), positions 3 apart always have a dot product of 1.96, whether they are positions 0 and 3 or 40 and 43.

It’s also the same for \(+k\) and \(-k\), since cosine doesn’t care about sign. On their own, the dot products can’t tell “3 words before” from “3 words after”. The rotation above can, which is one reason the learned \(W_Q\) and \(W_K\) matter.

Why 10000, and why so many speeds?

The speeds are \(\omega_i = 1 / 10000^{2i/d}\), so the wavelengths grow geometrically from \(2\pi\) (about 6 positions) to \(10000 \cdot 2\pi\) (about 63,000 positions).

Think of the hands of a clock. The fast hand tells neighbouring positions apart, but it repeats every few steps. The slow hands barely move between neighbours, but they tell far-apart positions apart. Together, every position gets a unique pattern, and 10000 makes the slowest wave far longer than any sentence the model will see.

Learned positions work too

The paper also tried simply learning a vector for each position, like a second embedding table. The results were nearly identical (Table 3, row E). The authors kept the waves because they hoped the model could then handle sentences longer than any it saw in training.

Later models went both ways. BERT and GPT-2 learned their positions. Many of today’s models use RoPE (Su et al., 2021), which takes the rotation above literally: it rotates each query and key by its position, so a score depends only on the distance between the two words.

Many heads cost the same as one

Each head has its own \(W_Q\), \(W_K\) and \(W_V\), each of size \(d \times (d/h)\). Over \(h\) heads that is \(3 \cdot h \cdot d \cdot (d/h) = 3d^2\) weights, plus \(d^2\) for \(W_O\):

\[4d^2 \text{ weights, whatever } h \text{ is.}\]

So splitting into heads is free. The paper tested this (Table 3, row A). One big head scored 0.9 BLEU worse than 8 heads. Too many heads hurt as well: with 32 heads of size 16, quality dropped again. Each head needs enough numbers to ask a useful question.

Further reading

  • Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need, sections 3.2.2 (multi-head), 3.5 (positions) and 4 (why self-attention).
  • Amirhossein Kazemnejad, Transformer Architecture: The Positional Encoding: a careful look at the rotation property.
  • Jesse Vig, BertViz: see what real attention heads learn.

entry.title: attention is all you need, part 1: self-attention from scratch

link.title: attention is all you need, part 1: self-attention from scratch

entry.content:
Series · Attention is all you need 1Self-attention from scratch 2Multi-head attention and positions 3One encoder block 4The decoder, masking and training 5Inference and the KV cache

In 2017 a team at Google published a paper with a bold title: Attention Is All You Need. It described the Transformer. Today almost every large language model, from ChatGPT to Claude, is built on it.

This series rebuilds the Transformer piece by piece. Every figure runs a real (but tiny) Transformer in your browser, and every number you see is computed, not drawn by hand. You can change the sentence and watch every matrix change with it.

This first part covers the idea at the heart of the paper: self-attention. In a previous post I treated the network as a black box that hands out scores. Now we open the box.

The toy model

Real models are huge: GPT-3 gives each word 12,288 numbers. Ours gives each word 8, so whole matrices fit on screen. The rest of the setup:

  • a vocabulary of about 30 words (press words it knows in the figure to see them),
  • attention with d_k = 4 numbers per query and key,
  • weights from a fixed random seed, except for one attention head that I wired by hand so it has a clear story to tell.

The model is not trained, so it can’t write a sentence. But the arithmetic is exactly the arithmetic of the paper. I checked it against PyTorch’s own Transformer layers, and they agree to within 10⁻¹⁴.

Scroll slowly. Inside each step, scrolling also plays the step: matrices fill in one cell at a time.

Self-attention, step by step

Before Transformers, language models were mostly recurrent networks (RNNs). They read a sentence like we do: one word at a time, left to right.

After each word, the RNN updates one memory vector, h. Everything it knows about the start of the sentence has to survive being passed down that chain.

Two problems follow. Long sentences get blurry, because early words fade from the memory. And it is slow, because word 6 can’t start until word 5 is done.

Attention throws the chain away. Every word gets to look straight at every other word, in one step.

The distance between the first and the last word is now the same as between neighbours: one hop. And all the pairs can be computed at the same time, which is what GPUs are good at.

The question is how much each word should look at each other word. That is what the next steps compute.

First, words become numbers. Each word in the vocabulary has an id, and the embedding table E has one row per id. We look up one row per word and stack them into a matrix X.

X has one row per word and 8 columns. In a real model the columns are learned and mean nothing we can name. In this toy I gave them names: noun, verb, animal, and so on. That makes it easier to see why the attention below comes out the way it does.

Each word asks a question. We multiply X by a weight matrix \(W_Q\) to get the queries \(Q = X W_Q\).

Watch the figure: row i of X times column j of \(W_Q\) gives cell (i, j) of Q. Multiply the pairs and add them up, as written at the bottom of the figure. That is all matrix multiplication is.

The wiring I chose means a verb’s query says “I’m looking for an animal” and a preposition’s query says “I’m looking for a thing”.

Two more matrices, the same trick. \(K = X W_K\) gives every word a key, and \(V = X W_V\) gives it a value.

A helpful picture is a library search:

  • the query is what you type into the search box,
  • each key is the label on a book’s spine,
  • each value is what is inside the book.

Queries are matched against keys. Values are what you take home.

Now we score every pair. The score for word i looking at word j is the dot product of query i and key j. Doing all pairs at once is one matrix product: \(Q K^\top\).

\(K^\top\) is K turned on its side, so its columns are the keys. The result is a square grid: one row per word asking, one column per word being asked.

A large dot product means the query and the key point the same way: a good match. Red cells are strong matches.

Then we shrink the scores, dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\). With \(d_k = 4\), that is a divide by 2.

Why? A dot product adds up \(d_k\) products. The more terms, the bigger the scores get (they grow like \(\sqrt{d_k}\)). Very big scores make the next step, softmax, put almost all the weight on one word. Then learning gets stuck.

Try the demo on the right. Random queries and keys, with \(d_k\) = 1024 and no division, hand nearly 100% to one word. Tick divide by √d_k and the spread comes back.

Where does \(\sqrt{d_k}\) come from? See why divide by √d_k further down.

Scores become weights. We apply softmax to each row. It makes every number positive and makes each row add up to exactly 1:

\[\text{softmax}(x)_i = \frac{e^{x_i}}{\sum_j e^{x_j}}\]

Now row i says how word i splits its attention: a percentage for every word in the sentence. Hover or tap a row label to see it as bars.

Look at sat: most of its attention goes to cat. The verb found who did the sitting.

Finally, we mix the values. Multiply the weights by V. Output row i is a blend of all the value rows, each in the amount given by row i of the weights.

So the new vector for sat is mostly cat’s value, plus a little of everything else. Each word has gathered information from the words that matter to it.

The output has one row per word, just like X. That’s important: it means we can stack these layers, as part 3 shows.

Here is the whole head at a glance. Each line goes from a word asking (left) to a word being asked (right). Thicker lines mean more attention.

Hover a word on the left. Then try your own sentence in the box above: “the quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog” or “my dog chased a ball in the park”.

Adjectives find their nouns, verbs find animals, prepositions find things. In a trained model nobody wires this by hand. It is learned from data, and some heads really do learn patterns like these.

The whole thing in one line

Everything the figure did is the paper’s equation (1):

\[\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q K^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V\]

with \(Q = X W_Q\), \(K = X W_K\) and \(V = X W_V\). Reading it from the inside out:

  1. \(Q K^\top\): score every query against every key.
  2. \(\div \sqrt{d_k}\): keep the scores in a sensible range.
  3. softmax: turn each row of scores into weights that sum to 1.
  4. \(\times V\): mix the values with those weights.

It is called scaled dot-product attention. It is self-attention when queries, keys and values all come from the same sentence, as here. In part 4 we’ll meet cross-attention, where the queries come from one sentence and the keys and values from another.

What’s still missing

Two things in our figure should bother you.

  • Word order. Nothing in these steps knows where a word is. Shuffle the sentence and each word gets exactly the same output, just in a different row. (Try “mat the on sat cat the”.)
  • One question per word. A single head can only look for one kind of thing at a time. sat wants to know who sat and where.

The paper fixes both, with positional encodings and multi-head attention. That is part 2.

Going deeper

The steps above show what happens. This section is about why. Each question stands on its own, so skip to the ones you care about.

Why divide by √d_k?

Picture a fresh model, before any training. Its weights are random, so the numbers in each query and key behave like independent random numbers with mean 0 and variance 1.

A score is a dot product: \(q \cdot k = q_1 k_1 + q_2 k_2 + \dots + q_{d_k} k_{d_k}\).

  • Each product \(q_i k_i\) has mean 0 and variance \(1 \times 1 = 1\).
  • The variances of independent terms add up. With \(d_k\) terms, the variance of \(q \cdot k\) is \(d_k\).
  • So the typical size of a score (its standard deviation) is \(\sqrt{d_k}\).

This is footnote 4 of the paper. With the paper’s \(d_k = 64\), raw scores are typically around ±8. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) brings the spread back to about 1, whatever \(d_k\) is.

Try it below. The left panel keeps a fixed axis, so you can watch the raw scores spread out as \(d_k\) grows. The right panel, after dividing, keeps the same shape.

Why a big spread is bad. Softmax turns scores into weights. Its gradient, how much weight \(p_i\) moves when score \(x_j\) moves, is

\[\frac{\partial p_i}{\partial x_j} = p_i\,(\delta_{ij} - p_j)\]

where \(\delta_{ij}\) is 1 if \(i = j\) and 0 otherwise. When one weight is close to 1 and the rest are close to 0, every one of these terms is close to 0. For the winner, \(p_i(1 - p_i) \approx 0\). For everyone else, \(p_i \approx 0\).

So almost no gradient flows back to \(W_Q\) and \(W_K\), and attention stops learning. In the paper’s words, large dot products “push the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients”. The table in the figure measures this: at \(d_k = 1024\) without the division, the top word takes about 98% and the gradient is more than ten times smaller than with it.

One caveat: the “independent, variance 1” picture is exact only at the start of training. Trained queries and keys are not random. But the start is exactly where it matters. A model that can’t take its first steps never learns anything.

Why not divide by d_k?

That over-corrects. The spread would become \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\): about 0.125 for \(d_k = 64\). Scores that small make the softmax nearly flat, so every word gets about the same weight and attention can’t pick anything out. \(\sqrt{d_k}\) is the one divisor that keeps the spread at 1 for every size.

There is a twist. After training, queries and keys are no longer independent, and their dot products can grow like \(d_k\) rather than \(\sqrt{d_k}\). For that reason, some recipes for very wide models (μP, Yang et al., 2022) do divide by \(d_k\).

A dot product, or a small network?

Before the Transformer, the popular choice was additive attention (Bahdanau et al., 2014). It scores a pair with a tiny neural network, \(v^\top \tanh(W_1 q + W_2 k)\), instead of a dot product.

The paper says the two work about equally well in theory, but dot products are much faster, because all the scores come out of one matrix multiplication. It also notes that without scaling, additive attention beat dot-product attention for larger \(d_k\). The authors suspected the large-dot-product problem above, which is why they added the \(\sqrt{d_k}\).

Why two matrices, W_Q and W_K?

Why not one matrix W for both queries and keys? Then the score of word i looking at word j would be \(x_i W W^\top x_j\), which is exactly the score of j looking at i. Every attention pattern would be symmetric.

Language isn’t symmetric. In our hand-wired head, sat looks hard at cat (score 1.92), but cat barely looks at sat (score 0.02). The verb is searching for its subject; the noun isn’t searching for its verb. Separate \(W_Q\) and \(W_K\) let “what I’m looking for” differ from “what I offer”.

Why softmax?

We want weights that are positive and add up to 1, so the output is a weighted average of the values. Softmax gives that, and it is smooth, so gradients can flow through it. Picking only the top word (a “hard” max) has no useful gradient at all.

A handy property: adding the same number to every score in a row changes nothing, because it cancels between the top and bottom of the fraction. Code uses this to subtract each row’s maximum before taking \(e^x\), so the numbers never overflow. The toy model here does the same.

Further reading

  • Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need (2017). Section 3.2 covers everything in this post.
  • Jay Alammar, The Illustrated Transformer: the classic picture-book version.
  • Polo Club, Transformer Explainer: GPT-2 running live in your browser.
  • Harvard NLP, The Annotated Transformer: the paper, line by line, in PyTorch.

entry.title: how a language model picks the next word

link.title: how a language model picks the next word

entry.content:
You know the word suggestions above your phone keyboard? Type “see you” and it offers “soon”, “tomorrow”, “later”.

A chatbot works the same way, just much better. It never plans a whole answer. It only asks one question, over and over:

Given the text so far, what should come next?

It picks one piece, adds it to the end, and asks again. That’s it. Poems, code and exam answers all come from this one loop.

This post walks through the loop step by step. There are two figures you can play with. Their numbers are a toy I made up by hand, but the steps are the same ones real models use.

The loop

Every reply is built like this:

  1. Read the text so far.
  2. Score every possible next piece. (This is the neural network’s job.)
  3. Turn the scores into chances.
  4. Pick one piece.
  5. Add it to the text, and go back to step 1.

The loop stops when the model picks a special “the end” piece, or runs out of room.

We won’t open up the neural network here. Think of it as a black box that hands us a list of scores.

The pieces are called tokens

I keep saying “piece” because models don’t really use words. They use tokens: chunks of text from a fixed list. Common words are one token. Long or rare words get split up.

The ␣ means “starts with a space”. To the model, ␣cat and cat are two different tokens.

The list of all tokens is the vocabulary. A real one has around 50,000 to 250,000 tokens. For the rest of this post I’ll mostly say “word” anyway, because it’s easier to read.

Step 1: score every word

Take the prompt “The cat sat on the”. The model gives every word in its vocabulary a score. A higher score means “this fits better”. The score has a name, a logit, but it’s just a number.

Scores are hard to read alone. Is 3.1 good? Only if the others are lower. What we want instead are chances: numbers between 0% and 100% that add up to 100%.

Softmax: scores into chances

The tool for this is called softmax. It does two things:

  1. Make every score positive, in a way that stretches out the gaps. (It raises the number e ≈ 2.718 to the power of each score.)
  2. Divide each result by the total, so they add up to 100%.

Here it is with three words:

The best word stays on top, and every word gets some chance. One more useful fact: only the gaps between scores matter. Add 10 to every score and the chances don’t move.

For the curious, the formula is

\[p_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_{j} e^{z_j}}\]

where \(z_i\) is the score of word \(i\). You don’t need it for the rest of the post.

Temperature: the “creativity” knob

Many AI tools have a temperature setting. Before softmax, every score is divided by the temperature.

  • Low temperature (below 1) makes the gaps bigger. The favourite wins even more often. Output gets safe and predictable.
  • Temperature 1 leaves the scores as they are.
  • High temperature (above 1) makes the gaps smaller. Unlikely words get more of a chance. Output gets more varied, and sometimes weird.

Notice that mat is always first. Temperature never changes the order. It only changes how far ahead the leader is.

There’s no deep theory behind the “right” temperature. People just try values and see what reads well. Stephen Wolfram, in his ChatGPT essay, found that about 0.8 worked best for essays.

Try it yourself. Drag the temperature slider, then press Pick a word a few times.

How unsure is the model?

The “uncertainty” chart in Figure 1 measures how spread out the chances are. It’s called entropy, and it’s counted in bits.

  • 0 bits: one word has all the chance. The model is sure.
  • 3 bits: all eight words are equally likely. That’s as unsure as three coin flips.

Our toy sits at 2.29 bits at temperature 1, and drops to almost 0 at temperature 0.1.

Step 2: pick a word

Now we have chances. We still need to choose one word. The rule for choosing is called the decoding strategy. Here are the common ones.

Greedy: always take the top word. Same prompt, same answer, every time. The downside is that it gets stuck. On long texts it often repeats itself, because once a loop is the most likely path, nothing breaks it out. (Set Figure 1 to top 1 to see greedy.)

Sampling: roll a weighted die. Each word’s chance of coming up equals its probability. At temperature 1, mat comes up about 41% of the time, floor about 22%, and once in a while keyboard. Press Pick 50 times in the figure. The Sampled bars start out bumpy, then slowly match the Model probability bars.

Top-k and top-p: cut off the junk first. A real vocabulary has 100,000+ tokens, and most are nonsense in any given spot. Each is unlikely, but together they add up. So before sampling, we throw most of them away:

  • Top-k keeps only the k best words. Set the figure to top 3 and you get 53.1%, 29.2% and 17.7%, the same three numbers as the softmax example above.
  • Top-p keeps the best words until their chances add up to p, say 90%. At temperature 1 that keeps five words (mat to roof) and drops keyboard, moon and banana.

Top-p is clever because it adapts. When the model is sure, a couple of words already reach 90%. When it’s unsure, more words get in. That’s why many tools use top-p with a medium temperature.

A simple way to remember it: temperature changes how steep the odds are; top-k and top-p change how many words are allowed to play.

Step 3: repeat

Once a word is picked, it joins the text, and the model scores the next spot from scratch. So a whole sentence is a path through a tree of choices.

Chances multiply along a path

To get the chance of a whole path, multiply the chance of each step. For the most common path, time → , → there → was:

Even the most popular opening comes out word for word only about 1 time in 7. Each extra word multiplies in another number below 1, so any exact long text is very unlikely.

(Multiplying hundreds of tiny numbers gets so close to zero that computers lose track. So in practice, models add up the logarithms of the chances instead. Same answer, safer maths.)

No going back

A real model has a branch for every token in its vocabulary. With 100,000 tokens, ten steps already give more possible paths than anyone could ever list. So the model never looks at the whole tree. It walks one step at a time, without looking ahead.

That means early choices steer everything after. Pick midnight instead of time in Figure 2 and every later column changes. The model can’t go back and edit an earlier word. It can only keep adding new ones.

What this explains about chatbots

Knowing the loop makes a lot of chatbot behaviour make sense:

  • Same question, different answers. Sampling takes a different path each time. Turn the temperature near 0 and answers become much more repeatable.
  • “Creative” vs “precise” modes. That’s usually just the temperature knob, sometimes with top-p.
  • Repeating itself. Greedy picking and very low temperatures can fall into loops.
  • Confident mistakes. The model picks words that fit, one at a time. Nothing in the loop checks if the whole answer is true. A smooth wrong answer and a smooth right one look the same to it.
  • Wording matters. Your prompt is the start of the path. Change a few words and the very first scores change, and so does everything after.

Summary

  • A model writes by repeating one step: score every token, turn scores into chances, pick one, add it.
  • Softmax turns scores into chances. Only the gaps between scores matter.
  • Temperature makes the odds steeper (low) or flatter (high). It never changes the order.
  • Greedy, sampling, top-k and top-p are different rules for picking.
  • A full reply is a path through a tree. Early picks shape everything after.

Real models do exactly this, just with 100,000+ tokens instead of eight words, and a huge neural network making the scores. How that network works is a story for another post.
